headline: A Denver man is trapping and egging Waymo’s self-driving cars, police say
author: Grey Battle

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
The Waymo eggings follow a pattern, Denver police say.

First, the middle-aged man parks his silver Toyota Corolla in front of one of the self-driving cars, stopping the vehicle from moving, a police report says. Then, police say, the man takes orange road cones out of his trunk and places them in front of the Waymo so it can’t move.
The man often then pelts the robotic car with eggs and drives away, leaving the Waymo trapped, the police report says.
An investigator working for Waymo told police the company has recorded 30 incidents of a bearded, ponytailed man trapping and egging its vehicles.

Matt Jablow, a spokesperson for the Denver District Attorney’s Office, said in a statement that his office would work with the city attorney’s office “to identify the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop.”

Since Waymo launched in Denver in September 2025, the vehicles have driven past barricades into a farmers market, come close to driving over a freshly paved road and received a parking ticket, local television station 9News reported.
But Mayor Mike Johnston said this week that Waymo cars are mostly working well in Denver.
“They’re popular, energy-friendly, efficient, and affordable,” he said in a statement. “There have been a few expected hiccups here and there, but overall they’re a good egg.”
Virginia sheriff’s office ends agreement with ICE after court ruling

The sheriff’s office in Loudoun County, Virginia, this week ended its cooperation agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after an appeals court upheld a state law limiting local law enforcement cooperation with immigration agents.

Virginia was one of several states this year to place restrictions on participation in ICE’s 287(g) program, which allows state and local officials to be deputized to conduct immigration enforcement. A federal judge temporarily blocked the provision from taking effect in July after the Justice Department sued, but a federal appeals court Monday reversed that decision.

The Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office entered into a 287(g) agreement last year, authorizing its officers to execute ICE administrative warrants, known as detainers, on individuals already in the sheriff’s custody. In an email, sheriff’s office spokesman Tom Julia said the department will abide by the court’s decision. He said the department no longer will keep an individual scheduled for released in custody based on an ICE warrant, but it will continue to honor immigration warrants that are “concurrent” with a person’s release.

So far this year, ICE has issued 673 detainers for noncitizen inmates in the Loudoun County jail, of whom 330 were transferred to ICE custody, according to Julia. The sheriff’s office has not released anyone to ICE since the appeals court ruling, he said.
The agreement had long been a point of contention between Loudoun Sheriff Mike Chapman and the county’s Democratic-controlled board of supervisors.

Loudoun County Board Chair Phyllis J. Randall said in a statement that she was “very pleased” by the sheriff’s decision, adding: “Across our country, poorly trained ICE agents have wreaked havoc, caused death, killed American citizens and terrorized American cities.”
Latin American researcher
Mexico condemns DEA tip line asking people to report corrupt officials in Sinaloa

MEXICO CITY — The Mexican government presented a formal complaint to the U.S. Embassy in Mexico after the Drug Enforcement Administration promoted a tip line for information that would help “expose corruption” and “dismantle narcoterrorist organizations.”

DEA chief Terry Cole, in a post Wednesday on X, shared a dedicated tip line now available in Sinaloa to report alleged members of designated foreign terrorist organizations, corrupt government officials and criminal networks involved in money laundering. Another line will be opened for Jalisco state, he said.

In response, Mexican Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco presented a formal complaint to U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson in an effort to defend Mexico’s sovereignty, President Claudia Sheinbaum said. The DEA did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

“We have made it very clear to the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination,” Sheinbaum said during her Friday morning news conference. She described the tip line as a form of U.S. “interference” in Mexico.

While Mexico accepts its responsibility to stop drugs from crossing the border, Sheinbaum said, the U.S. also has a responsibility to reduce drug use among its own population and to detain the cartel members distributing drugs and laundering money within U.S. territory.

The spat comes after the Mexican government, aided by intelligence gleaned by U.S. drones, arrested one of the FBI’s 10 most-wanted fugitives in Sinaloa. Pressured by President Donald Trump’s administration to do more against cartels, Mexico has increased its security operations in Sinaloa, where a violent turf war has taken place after the U.S. arrested drug kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada.
Reporter covering issues in national K-12 education
Illinois will not opt in to federal school voucher program
Illinois will not participate in the nation’s new voucher-style federal tax credit program when it launches in January, Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker said this week.

Pritzker, a possible 2028 presidential contender, echoed objections voiced by many Democrats, saying voucher programs subsidize tuition for families already in private schools and take money from public schools.

“At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education — especially as the Trump Administration’s policies decimate education,” Pritzker said in a statement.

The new program puts Democratic governors who oppose vouchers in a political conundrum. It will let taxpayers donate to certain nonprofits, which will then give scholarships to private school families for tuition. The program also allows funds to go to public school students for services such as tutoring.
The federal government will reimburse eligible taxpayers for every dollar they donate, up to $1,700, via a tax credit. Governors must opt their states into the program.
Most states that plan to take part are led by Republicans.
A growing cohort of left-leaning advocates says governors who do not opt in are passing up billions of dollars that can help public schools.

Pritzker’s “decision is precisely how Democrats squander the opportunity that emerged from the recent election: focusing on fighting Trump so much that we become more driven to oppose him than to deliver for our constituents,” Jorge Elorza, chief executive of Democrats for Education Reform, said in a statement.

Reporter covering the military and national security
U.S. military jet disables commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman
A U.S. military jet fired a precision munition into the stern of a commercial ship Thursday in the Gulf of Oman and disabled it, U.S. Central Command said Friday in a statement.

The Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer had departed from Bandar Abbas, a port city in Iran, and was attempting to run the naval blockade the U.S. is enforcing on any ship departing Iran as a way to cut off Tehran’s revenue. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s approach to try forcing Iran to concede after more than nine months of military operations since the U.S. and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury in February.
The strike disabled the ship but did not harm the crew, Central Command said.
The U.S. has maintained a significant naval presence in the Arabian Sea and Gulf of Oman to stop any vessels carrying Iranian oil or other exports from leaving the country.
Reporter covering Russia
‘GTA VI’ release has swept PlayStation 5 off the shelves worldwide
The release of the highly anticipated “Grand Theft Auto VI” game has caused a worldwide shortage of gaming consoles, sweeping shelves from the United States to Japan.

The Rockstar Games crime epic, 13 years in the making, came out last week and is playable only on the Xbox Series X or S and PlayStation 5, the most recent generation of consoles from Microsoft and Sony.
The game landed in an already strained market, where console manufacturers have been hit hard by a global memory chip shortage caused by AI companies buying up components.

In the United States, Sony’s higher-end PlayStation 5 Pro was intermittently sold out even before the release, with major retailers out of stock at its $900 retail price and resellers asking as much as $1,900.

In Germany, stores such as MediaMarkt and Saturn are sold out of PS5 models and lower-end Xbox ones. Private-sale platforms are flooded with ads from people looking to buy used consoles at the price of new. Consoles at Sony-recommended prices are similarly hard to find in other European countries, with third-party resellers offering the device at nearly double the price.

In Japan, Sony has gone as far as restricting who is allowed to buy the console to block scalpers. The Sony Store sells it only through a lottery open to buyers with a Japanese account and at least 60 hours of verified PS4 or PS5 playtime.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
GOP governors invite Texans to move to their states to flee blue wave
HOUSTON — Republican governors have a message for conservative Texans upset by Democrats sweeping every statewide office: “Texit” and move here!
Sen. Tommy Tuberville, Alabama’s governor-elect, tweeted this week, telling any “red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas … Alabama is open for business.”
Not to be outdone, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry then posted a photo of new billboards he erected in Texas saying: “If you’re from Louisiana, it’s time to come home!”
“Louisiana is leading the nation in economic opportunity,” Landry wrote. “Come home and fill these new job opportunities!”
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt then urged conservative Texans to defect across the northern state line.

“Hey Texans, Oklahoma is open for business, committed to conservative values, and ready to welcome families and entrepreneurs,” Stitt said in a post on X. “Come build your American Dream in Oklahoma!”
Texans — Democrat and Republican alike — had thoughts.
Rep. Joaquin Castro, who as a Texas state lawmaker in 2003 fled to Oklahoma with other Democrats to block Republican congressional redistricting, called Stitt’s invitation “thoughtful” and “kind.”
“I can attest the state was incredibly welcoming,” he said.

Those who rejected the GOP pitch noted that Texas has no state income tax and leads the country in gross domestic product growth and job creation. Others responded with links to Facebook groups offering help to conservative Texans who want to relocate.
“We Texans should all consider Florida or Tennessee now, too,” one retiree in the Houston suburbs posted.
